analysis.one_liner: Stops employer health plans from giving dialysis worse coverage to shift costs onto Medicare.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to protect dialysis patients from cutbacks in employer health plans died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend Medicare law so that employer and other group health plans cannot single out dialysis patients for less generous benefits, directly or indirectly, or push the primary cost of their care onto Medicare. It responds to plans that, after recent litigation, have limited dialysis coverage to save money. The bill also preserves one tool plans keep: they may still choose which dialysis clinics are in their provider networks.
analysis.who_benefits: People with end stage renal disease who rely on employer or group health plans before turning to Medicare. The bill would guarantee them the same benefit design as other enrollees, rather than facing coverage engineered to make dialysis unattractive, and would keep their private plan as the primary payer instead of Medicare.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Dialysis patients on employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars group health plans from differentiating benefits between people with end stage renal disease or needing dialysis and everyone else, whether directly or indirectly [S2].
It states its purpose as prohibiting plans from shifting primary responsibility for covering dialysis patients' care onto Medicare, so private plans must remain the first payer [S2].
It would require the Secretary of Health and Human Services to enforce the rule through the existing nonconformance determination process, giving the protection an enforcement mechanism [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers and group health plan sponsors, and indirectly their enrollees through premiums, would bear higher costs for dialysis coverage instead of shifting that cost onto Medicare. Health insurers lose flexibility to design benefits around expensive dialysis claims.

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly preserves plans' ability to limit which dialysis providers are in their networks, so patients could still face a restricted choice of clinics even as benefit discrimination is barred [S2].
Dialysis care is extremely expensive, and requiring plans to cover it on equal terms raises costs that group plans would spread across employers and all enrollees through premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real and targeted at a documented cost-shifting practice, and the network carve-out shows an effort to answer plans' management concerns. The cost is higher premiums spread across group plans, which is modest per enrollee but concentrated on employers. On balance it is a narrowly drawn patient protection rather than a broad expansion.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2024, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and Congress ended in January 2025 with the committee never acting on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on September 11, 2024, joined by Sens. Booker and Heinrich, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee [S1][S2][S4].
The bill ended the Congress with two cosponsors from Senate Democrats and one from Senate Republicans, a small bipartisan group [S3].
No further action appears in the record after the referral to Finance; no markup, no floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors are better off: without the bill, plans can keep limiting dialysis benefits and steering primary coverage of dialysis patients toward Medicare. Dialysis patients got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee, where he is a member.

for.name: Sens. Booker and Heinrich
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its Democratic sponsors.

for.name: 2 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small bipartisan base.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over Medicare
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup or a vote before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start, a Republican lead with two Democratic senators at introduction and cosponsors split 2-1 across the parties, but only three senators in total signed on.

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: The bill would bar plans from designing benefits to disfavor dialysis patients and from shifting the primary cost of their care to Medicare, and would let regulators find plans out of compliance if they do. It carves out network decisions, so plans keep one lever for managing dialysis costs [S2].

With private plans required to pay for dialysis on equal terms rather than disfavoring it, dialysis clinics keep a larger private-payer revenue base instead of seeing patients pushed to Medicare's lower payment rates.

Employer plans would absorb the cost of dialysis coverage on equal terms rather than engineering benefits around it, raising plan costs. Plans' cost control in this area came directly at dialysis patients' expense, so the industry interest ran against the patients in this bill.
